lessons.title: Case Study: Trend-Following Applied to Nifty, Gold, and Crude Simultaneously

body.text: None of the last two lessons' arguments mean much until you actually watch three unrelated markets trend, or fail to, at different times, and see the combined book come out smoother than any one of them individually managed to be on its own.

children.text: This lesson applies Lesson 2's vol-scaled time-series momentum signal to three genuinely different markets, Nifty 50 futures, MCX Gold, and Crude, over 2018 to 2023, a period that includes a global pandemic crash, a historic oil market dislocation, and a sharp equity recovery. The point is not to prove trend-following is flawless, Lesson 5 covers exactly where it fails, but to make the diversification-of-bets argument from Lesson 1 concrete rather than abstract.
Setting Up the Case Study: 2018 to 2023, Three Markets

Each market runs the identical 12-month look-back, volatility-scaled signal from Lesson 2, sized to a common risk target, with no asset-specific tuning of any kind. Nifty was chosen as this course's core equity proxy, gold as the classic stress-period diversifier from Chapter 1, and crude as the most volatile, least stable-curve commodity covered in Chapter 2, deliberately including the market most likely to produce the messiest individual result.

children.text: Reading the Individual Signals: When Each Market Trended

Each market's best trending periods landed at different times. Nifty's clearest sustained trend ran through the 2020 to 2021 recovery covered in Chapter 1's opening example, then whipsawed through the choppy 2022 range this course has referenced repeatedly. Gold trended cleanly upward through 2019 into mid-2020, exactly the stress-period behavior Chapter 1 flagged. Crude produced the most dramatic single event of the period: on April 20, 2020, WTI crude futures traded negative for the first time in history, as collapsing demand met a storage capacity crunch right at contract expiry, an extraordinary illustration of Chapter 2's point that crude's storage economics can dominate its price in ways gold's never do. A trend system, positioned short crude heading into that collapse, captured a genuinely historic move that had nothing to do with equities or gold at all.
The Combined Portfolio: Diversification of Bets in Practice

None of the three individual signals in the illustrative table above is remarkable on its own, Sharpe ratios in the 0.30 to 0.45 range are respectable but unspectacular. The combined, equal risk-weighted book comes out meaningfully higher than any individual signal and higher than a simple average of the three would suggest, which is the Fundamental Law of Active Management from Lesson 1 showing up directly in the numbers. A subtlety worth flagging: the correlation between these three trend signals' returns is typically even lower than the correlation between the underlying assets' raw returns, since a trend signal can be long, short, or flat depending on each market's own regime, which decorrelates the strategies' outcomes further than the assets' prices alone would.

children.text: A Period Where All Three Agreed: March 2020

Diversification of bets does not mean the signals never agree, and March 2020 is the clearest example of when they should. As the COVID crash unfolded, a trend system already positioned would have been turning short Nifty and short crude as both markets broke down, while its gold position, already trending upward from 2019, continued working. This is trend-following's crisis-alpha property from Lesson 1 made concrete: the system was not fighting the crash the way a fixed long-only book was, it was positioned in the direction each individual market was already moving, asset class by asset class.

body.text: The goal of combining trend signals across asset classes is not to guarantee they never move together. It is to ensure that when they do move together, in a genuine systemic event like March 2020, they are more likely to be reinforcing the same profitable direction than randomly canceling each other out, since each signal is independently reading its own market's regime rather than following a single shared assumption.

body.title: The Combined Book That Beat All Its Parts
body.scenario: A quant researcher reviews this lesson's illustrative results and is puzzled: the combined portfolio's Sharpe ratio, roughly 0.75, is higher not just than any individual signal, but higher than what a simple average of the three individual Sharpe ratios, roughly 0.37, would suggest. They ask whether this must be a backtesting error, since combining three mediocre strategies should not obviously produce a clearly better one.
body.prompt: Is this pattern necessarily a sign of an error? What would you check to confirm the result is genuine rather than a mistake?
body.modelAnswer: This pattern is not necessarily an error, and is in fact exactly what the Fundamental Law of Active Management from Lesson 1 predicts when combining several bets that are not just individually profitable but also close to independent of each other. Combining strategies does not average their Sharpe ratios, it can meaningfully exceed a naive average specifically because uncorrelated return streams reduce combined volatility more than they reduce combined return. What should be checked to rule out an error is whether the three individual trend signals were genuinely computed independently and correctly, without any shared look-ahead bias or data leakage across markets, and whether the correlation between the three signals' actual return streams, not just the underlying assets' price correlation, is as low as the result implies. If those checks hold, the elevated combined Sharpe ratio is a real breadth effect, not a bug.

body.title: Signal Correlation vs Asset Correlation
body.question: According to this lesson, why can the correlation between two trend signals' returns be lower than the correlation between the underlying assets' raw price returns?
options: Because trend signals are always uncorrelated by mathematical definition
Because a trend signal can be long, short, or flat depending on each asset's own regime, which decorrelates the strategies' outcomes beyond what the assets' price correlation alone would suggest
Because trend signals only use fundamental data, not price data
Because Nifty and crude are never correlated in any way
body.explanation: A trend signal's return depends not just on how correlated the underlying assets are, but on whether the signals happen to be positioned in the same direction, opposite directions, or flat at any given time, since each signal independently reads its own asset's regime. This additional layer of independence is why combined trend portfolios can show even lower internal correlation than the raw asset correlation matrix from Chapter 3 would suggest on its own.

points: Applying the same vol-scaled trend signal to Nifty, Gold, and Crude with no asset-specific tuning produces genuinely different individual results, each market trending at a different time
Crude's April 2020 negative-price event is a concrete illustration of Chapter 2's point that crude's storage economics can dominate its price in extraordinary ways gold's never do

The combined, equal risk-weighted portfolio's Sharpe ratio meaningfully exceeded both any individual signal and a simple average of the three, the Fundamental Law of Active Management showing up directly in the numbers
Trend signal returns can be even less correlated with each other than the underlying assets' raw price returns, since each signal independently reads its own market's regime
March 2020 showed trend-following's crisis-alpha property concretely: the system was positioned with each individual market's own trend, not fighting a single shared assumption
None of this makes trend-following flawless; Lesson 5 covers the whipsaw and drawdown costs this same case study's markets also produced at other points in the period
